title: The General's Mountain: Hirafu, Kutchan and the Making of a Ski Town
standfirst: A volcanic cone the Ainu and later the Wajin both named after old legends, a homestead cut from raw forest in 1892, and a station that has sent skiers up the same mountain trail since the 1920s: this dossier follows Kutchan's Hirafu district, and its neighbour the renamed town of Niseko, from settlement to the powder-snow resort of today.

paragraphs.text: This ground is young volcanic country. The regional survey used elsewhere in this series classes almost the whole study area as either old volcanic apron or volcanic foot-slope, built up from the eruptions of the near-symmetrical cone that rises to the south-east. A 1924 ski guidebook published by the Railway Ministry already called that cone by the nickname still used today, Ezo-Fuji, "for its trim, elegant, truncated-cone shape" — and by its Ainu-derived name, Makkari-nupuri. A widely repeated local tradition ties the mountain's more formal name to something older still: the eighth-century chronicle Nihon Shoki records the general Abe no Hirafu leading a fleet of some 180 ships on a campaign in 658 CE that reportedly set up an administrative base called "Kōhō Yōtei." Wajin settlers matched that ancient name to this mountain and wrote it with the same characters, 後方羊蹄 — read in one tradition as Shiribeshi-yama, in the other, using the same characters' Chinese-derived sound, as Yōtei-zan.

The same legend gave a neighbouring settlement its name. Hirafu, a district of Kutchan today served by its own station, is said locally to preserve Abe no Hirafu's own name, and a Hirafu Shrine was built in 1912 to mark the tradition — though local historians themselves note that which of several rival towns, if any, the general's forces actually reached remains an open question; Yoichi, to the north, makes the same claim. Kutchan's own name has a separate, Ainu origin, usually explained as a place where water runs out through a narrow gorge; the characters 倶知安 were chosen for it in 1893 by a Hokkaido government official, Shirani Takeshi, the same year the settlement was registered as a village.

Kutchan's own account of its founding puts the date precisely: on 19 May 1892, a party led by Niki Takekichi, a settler from Tokushima Prefecture remembered locally as "the father of Kutchan's pioneering," together with Manabe Hamasaburō and others, entered the Kutchan wilderness and began felling the oak and Japanese cottonwood forest tree by tree. The village was formally established the following year, 1893; a branch office of neighbouring Abuta village's administration opened in Kutchan in 1895, and in 1896 — while the settlement was still, by its own telling, enduring a harsh pioneering existence — its first school, Kutchan Jinjō Elementary, opened its doors.

Growth followed the railway. When the Hokkaido Railway (today's JR Hakodate Main Line) reached the district on 15 October 1904, Kutchan and Hirafu stations opened on the very same day, giving the mountain two railheads within a few kilometres of each other. In 1910 the government placed the seat of the newly formed Shiribeshi Subprefecture at Kutchan, and the settlement became a fully fledged town in 1916; further schools, including a junior high school, followed in 1922. A light railway to Kyōgoku, opened in 1919 to move produce and passengers, would itself become a period piece: the national government closed it in 1986, the same year Kutchan hosted a national athletics meet under the nickname "Ezofuji Kutchan." Agriculture, not tourism, defined the town for most of the twentieth century: its first "Industrial Tourism Festival," held in 1963, later became the potato festival the town still runs today, and a potato mascot born for its 1991 centenary still represents it.

A few kilometres away, in what was then Kaributo village, a very different kind of estate was taking shape. The novelist Arishima Takeo's father applied in 1898 for land in the Makaributo wilderness, and the farm his family built there grew until, in 1922, the year before his death, Arishima Takeo announced he was giving it to his tenant farmers outright, to be held in common rather than worked as rented land — an almost unheard-of act among Japanese landowners of the period. A mutual-aid credit union set up to run the shared farm in 1924 carried his idea forward for a generation.

The postwar land reform of 1949 finally converted the shared farm into private smallholdings, closing that chapter formally, and a memorial hall that admirers had built at the old farm office later burned down by accident in 1957. Reconstruction efforts begun in 1963 eventually led the town itself to build a proper museum on the same ground for the centenary of Arishima's birth; it opened in 1978 and stands there today — in Niseko-cho, Kutchan's neighbour, not in Kutchan itself, a reminder that the district's ski slopes and its most famous piece of land reform belong to two different, adjoining towns.

Modern skiing arrived in Japan only in January 1911, at Takada in Niigata, under the Austro-Hungarian military attaché Theodor von Lerch. Kutchan's own historical record places Lerch's party on Mount Yōtei within about a year of that, giving public ski demonstrations and attempting the mountain in April 1912 without reaching the top; a 1924 Railway Ministry guidebook, by contrast, dates a Lerch attempt to March of the following year. Whichever exact winter it was, the first recorded ski ascent to the summit did not come until 1919, when members of Hokkaido Imperial University's ski club made it to the top using crampons.

By 1924 the same guidebook could already send readers straight to Hirafu for the climb: a fare table lists third-class tickets from Otaru, Sapporo and Hakodate to Hirafu Station, and describes the recommended route up the mountain's western face — an eight-chō walk from the station into the town, then along the Sapporo highway to a climbing office at the trailhead, where the road coming down from Kutchan joined the same path, and from there some two ri (about eight kilometres) to the summit. The guide recommends this western, Hirafu-side approach precisely because it has "almost no cliffs and almost no avalanches," making for a satisfying climb with relatively little exertion, and it names Hirafu, Kutchan and three neighbouring settlements as already "good places to ski."

Kaributo's own name outlived its usefulness once tourism arrived. In July 1963 the mountains above the village were designated part of the Niseko-Shakotan-Otaru Coast Quasi-National Park, and visitors and officials alike began complaining that a park called "Niseko" had no obvious front door, since the town beneath it was still called Kaributo. The town assembly first debated renaming only the railway station; from February 1964 an advisory meeting of council members pushed the idea forward, and on 24 April 1964 the assembly formally proposed changing both the station's name and the town's own name to Niseko. When it put the station question to Japanese National Railways, the railway refused that part outright the following month, citing a standing rule against place names written entirely in katakana.

So the town changed its own name instead, over the objections of its neighbour: in August 1964 the mayors of four surrounding towns had to mediate a formal protest from Kutchan before Kaributo could proceed. On 1 October 1964 the town became Niseko-chō, only the second Japanese municipality ever to take an all-katakana name. The station followed years later, renamed Niseko on 1 April 1968 — the first station on the national railway to carry an all-katakana name of its own.

The Alps reached Kutchan before the Australians did, at least on paper: in February 1964, while inspecting the Winter Olympics in Switzerland, Kutchan's mayor proposed a sister-city tie with St Moritz, formalised later that year. Kutchan formally declared itself a "town of skiing" in December 1972, and it was Australian visitors, arriving for the same dry powder snow the 1924 guidebook had already praised, who eventually turned that identity into an industry: by the town's own account, foreign-led condominium development in the resort area took off from the late 2000s, land prices in the Hirafu area climbing with it. The town's overnight stays by foreign visitors rose to about 460,000 in the 2018 financial year, roughly two and a half times the 2009 figure, even as total visitor numbers recovered from a mid-1990s slump to top one and a half million a year.

The 2008 financial crisis and the 2011 earthquake briefly slowed construction, but investment resumed from the mid-2010s, increasingly from other parts of Asia as well as Australia, with one company typically developing an entire self-contained resort — hotels, condominiums, lifts and shops together — rather than single buildings, alongside a separate boom in staff housing in Kutchan's own town centre as the resort's workforce grew. By January, the month when the resident foreign population peaks, more than one in seven residents registered in the town is a foreign national. In October 2019 the G20 tourism ministers met at the Niseko Hanazono resort, within Kutchan, and issued the "Hokkaido Kutchan Declaration" on sustainable tourism, formally recognising a district that the town's own planners still describe as selling, above everything else, one "killer content": powder snow.

Hirafu Station still stands where it opened in 1904, and the road it once sent climbers along toward Mount Yōtei's climbing office is, in its essentials, the same route described in the 1924 guidebook. The Hirafu Shrine still marks the town's contested claim on Abe no Hirafu's name. What has changed is the scale: a settlement that Kutchan's own history remembers as raw forest cleared tree by tree in 1892, and that needed a mediated peace with its neighbour before that neighbour could even change its name in 1964, now draws close to half a million foreign guest-nights a year to the same mountainside, with a Shinkansen extension due to bring Kutchan a new station of its own within the decade.

It is worth remembering, walking or driving between the two, that "Niseko" as international visitors use the word today covers ground that Japanese administration still keeps carefully apart: the ski slopes above Hirafu, the station and the town hall belong to Kutchan, which fought in 1964 to keep its own name and identity distinct from its neighbour's; the Arishima farm, the 1964 renaming itself and the Niseko brand's own legal home belong to the separate town of Niseko-cho next door. The mountain the two towns share, and the marketing name that now covers both, sit on top of a boundary each town spent much of the twentieth century insisting on.

timeline.what: The Nihon Shoki records Abe no Hirafu's fleet reaching "Kōhō Yōtei"; local tradition, contested, ties this to the mountain and to Hirafu's name.
Niki Takekichi's party, with Manabe Hamasaburō and others, enters the Kutchan wilderness and begins clearing forest.
Kutchan is registered as a village; Shirani Takeshi chooses the characters 倶知安 for its name.
Arishima Takeo's father applies for land in the Makaributo wilderness, in what is now Niseko-cho.
Kaributo village separates from Makari village, taking its name from "Makaributo."
The Hokkaido Railway opens; Kutchan and Hirafu stations open the same day.
Shiribeshi Subprefecture's office opens at Kutchan.
Lt.-Col. Theodor von Lerch's party attempts Mount Yōtei on skis without reaching the summit; sources disagree on the exact year.
Hokkaido Imperial University's ski club makes the first recorded summit of Mount Yōtei.
Arishima Takeo gives his Kaributo farm to his tenant farmers, to be held in common.
Kaributo becomes Niseko-cho, Japan's second all-katakana municipality name, after a dispute with Kutchan.
Kaributo Station is renamed Niseko Station, the first all-katakana station name on the national railway.
Kutchan declares itself a "town of skiing."

caveats: Several internet-accessible NDL items likely to hold the district's fullest early history — a 1911 Usu-Abuta history and a 1908 Iburi-province overview among them — returned server errors from the NDL Lab API on every attempt in this session and so are not cited as sources here, only listed in furtherReading. As a result this dossier rests on one NDL source rather than the four or more usually sought; readers wanting deeper pre-1920 local detail should treat this as a starting point.

Sources disagree on the exact year of Lt.-Col. Lerch's Mount Yōtei ski attempt (Kutchan's own timeline gives April 1912; a 1924 Railway Ministry guidebook gives March 1913); this dossier states both rather than resolving the discrepancy.

The tradition connecting Hirafu and Mount Yōtei's name to the seventh-century general Abe no Hirafu is reported here as local tradition, not settled history; the sources used are explicit that which, if any, present-day town his expedition reached is disputed, and that Yoichi makes a competing claim.

This dossier could not independently confirm a specific recent figure for Australian guest-nights in Kutchan (a figure near 167,000-168,000 appears in town planning material); it cites instead the town's own 2018 total-foreign-guest-night figure (about 460,000), which was directly verifiable in a document opened in this session.
